frase_gancho.texto: Sixteen stone figures gathered together forever in front of six axes.

puente_narrativo.texto: Those jade axes cut nothing. Now look for a larger one, with the face of a supernatural jaguar and a cleft at the top of its head.

guion_corto.texto: This miniature scene comes from La Venta, in Tabasco, and it was discovered in 1955. It consists of sixteen little stone figures, between sixteen and twenty centimeters tall, standing in front of a row of six slender axes made of jade and serpentine. Fifteen of them face a central figure, carved from a different stone, who has his back to the axes. All of them have elongated heads, from intentional skull deformation, slanted eyes, and mouths with downturned corners. No one knows for certain what gathering it represents: a council, a ceremony, a coronation? What is certain is that the Olmec buried it on purpose and covered it with colored sands, so that the scene would stay fixed for a long time.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine that someone freezes a meeting in time. That is what this piece is: a complete scene, with characters, captured in a single instant and kept underground for more than two thousand six hundred years. It is Offering 4 of La Venta, and it is among the most famous in Mexican archaeology.

Let us see what is there. Sixteen small figures, standing in a row. Fifteen are made of jade, serpentine, or green stone; the central one is made of a different stone, of a lighter tone, and stands with its back to six axes that rise like stelae, or like small columns. The other figures look at it. We do not know who it is: a chief, a god, a priest, someone being judged, a king taking power?

That is the question no one has been able to answer. Several ideas have been proposed: a council of lineage chiefs, an enthronement ceremony, a ritual assembly, a trial. Each specialist reads the scene differently. It is a theater of miniatures that no one has managed to read entirely, and perhaps that is its charm: whoever sees it completes the story on their own.

Look at the heads. All of them are elongated, backward and upward, because from infancy the skull was shaped with small boards. You already saw this custom in the introduction hall, among the skulls with deformation and the filed teeth, and you will see it again in the Maya Hall, in the profile of [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal). It was a way of saying who you were: the head as a sign of belonging or of prestige. And the faces share the Olmec mouth with downturned corners, which you already saw in the babies of Tlatilco and in the boy of Las Limas.

The most extraordinary thing is what they did afterward. The Olmec did not leave the offering in view: they buried it on purpose, in a pit, and covered it with layers of colored sands, white, yellow, and red. It was not made for anyone to admire. It was made to exist underground, like a seed. In the Mesoamerican world, to bury was to sow: to give the earth what was most precious, so that it would return what the people needed. The Mexica would do the same at the Templo Mayor, two thousand years later, with hundreds of offerings.

La Venta was the Olmec capital that followed San Lorenzo. It stood on an island surrounded by swamps, in Tabasco, and there a great clay pyramid was built, one of the first great constructions of Mesoamerica. It also had four colossal heads, sisters of the one you saw at the beginning of the hall. And beneath its courtyards, like this one, jade offerings carefully buried were found.

This offering was discovered in 1955, during an expedition that explored La Venta. Imagine it: the archaeologists were removing the earth and suddenly the figures appeared, just as they had been left almost three thousand years earlier, looking at one another. It is one of those images that stay with you: a conversation that no one heard, and that no one has stopped wanting to understand.

texto: Count the figures and find the one that is different from the others
Observe the elongated shape of the heads
Find the six axes and notice how they are arranged

texto.Origin: La Venta, municipality of Huimanguillo, Tabasco
texto.Dimensions: Statuettes: 0.16 to 0.20 m tall; axes: 0.23 to 0.27 m tall
texto.Discovery: Discovered in 1955 by the archaeologist Eduardo Contreras in Complex A of La Venta

texto.pregunta: Myth: This offering is a sculpture made to be displayed.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was made to be buried: no one was meant to see it. What mattered was that it existed underground, not that it be admired.
